intro:
**Intro**

Back pain can feel like an unwelcome guest that never knows when to leave. The good news is that you don’t need expensive equipment or a trip to the clinic to find relief. With just a few minutes each day, you can *relieve back pain at home* using simple stretches that target tight muscles, improve flexibility, and promote better posture. Below are fifteen easy-to‑follow moves that fit into any schedule—whether you’re a busy professional, a stay‑at‑home parent, or anyone looking to feel more comfortable in their own skin.

---

sections.heading: Cat‑Cow Stretch
sections.body:
The Cat‑Cow stretch gently mobilizes the entire spine, easing tension in the lumbar and thoracic regions. Begin on all fours, hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Inhale as you drop your belly, lift your head and tailbone (Cow), then exhale to round your back, tucking the chin and pelvis (Cat).  

Repeating this fluid motion for 1–2 minutes helps increase spinal flexibility and encourages the natural rhythm of breathing, both of which are essential for anyone trying to **relieve back pain at home**.

sections.heading: Child’s Pose
sections.body:
Child’s Pose is a restorative position that lengthens the lower back while calming the nervous system. Kneel on the floor, sit back on your heels, and stretch your arms forward, lowering your chest toward the mat. Let your forehead rest gently on the ground.  

Hold for 30–60 seconds, breathing deeply. This simple pose releases pressure on the lumbar discs and can be a soothing way to transition between more active stretches.

sections.heading: Knee‑to‑Chest Stretch
sections.body:
Lying on your back, draw one knee toward your chest while keeping the opposite leg extended on the floor. Hug the thigh with both hands, feeling a gentle stretch in the lower back and glutes.  

Switch sides after 20–30 seconds. This stretch helps realign the pelvis and reduces the pulling sensation that often contributes to chronic back discomfort.

sections.heading: Supine Twist
sections.body:
Start on your back with arms stretched out to the sides, forming a “T.” Bend your knees, place your feet flat, and let them fall slowly to one side, keeping shoulders grounded.  

Hold for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. The supine twist gently rotates the spine, loosening tight muscles and improving mobility—key components for those who want to **relieve back pain at home**.

sections.heading: Pelvic Tilts
sections.body:
Pelvic tilts strengthen the core muscles that support the lower back. Lie on your back with knees bent, feet hip‑width apart. Gently press your lower back into the floor by engaging your abdominal muscles, then release.  

Perform 10–15 repetitions. This micro‑movement teaches your body how to maintain a neutral spine during daily activities, reducing strain on the back.

sections.heading: Seated Forward Fold
sections.body:
Sit on the floor with legs extended straight ahead. Inhale, lengthen the spine, then exhale as you hinge at the hips, reaching toward your toes. Keep the back flat and avoid rounding.  

Stay for 30 seconds, breathing into the stretch. The seated forward fold targets the hamstrings and lower back, helping to alleviate tightness that often exacerbates pain.

sections.heading: Hip Flexor Lunge
sections.body:
From a standing position, step one foot back into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor. Keep the front knee over the ankle and gently tuck the pelvis under to feel a stretch in the hip flexor and front of the thigh.  

Hold for 30 seconds each side. Tight hip flexors can pull the pelvis forward, increasing lumbar arch and discomfort; this stretch works to counteract that imbalance.

sections.heading: Standing Side Bend
sections.body: Stand tall with feet hip‑width apart. Raise your right arm overhead and gently lean to the left, feeling a stretch along the right side of the torso and lower back.
